notes.title: Introduction to C – revision sheet
notes.md:
## History
- BCPL (Martin Richards, 1967) → B (Ken Thompson, 1970) → **C (Dennis Ritchie, AT&T Bell Labs, 1972)**, written for UNIX
- K&R C (Kernighan & Ritchie book, 1978); ANSI C89 / ISO C90; C99 (// comments, long long, bool); C11; C17
- Middle-level language: high-level constructs + pointers, bit operations; portable; compiled; case-sensitive

## Structure of a C program
1. Documentation (comments `/* … */`)  2. Link section (`#include <stdio.h>`)  3. Definition (`#define PI 3.14`)
4. Global declarations  5. `main()` – execution starts here (exactly one)  6. User-defined functions
- Every statement ends with `;`; `return 0;` = success
- Build: preprocess (.i) → compile (.s) → assemble (.o/.obj) → link (.exe/a.out)

## Character set and tokens
- Letters, digits, special characters, white space (not in basic set: `$ @ \``)
- Escape sequences: `\n` newline, `\t` tab, `\b` backspace, `\r` carriage return, `\0` null, `\\` backslash, `\'`, `\"`
- Tokens: keywords (32 in C89), identifiers, constants, strings, operators, special symbols

## Constants, variables, data types
- Primary constants: integer (`-275`, `010` octal = 8, `0x1F` = 31), real (`3.2e-5`, type double), character (`'A'` = 65)
- Secondary: arrays, pointers, structures, unions, enums
- Identifiers: letters, digits, `_`; not starting with a digit; not a keyword; case-sensitive
- Sizes (typical 32-bit): char 1, short 2, int 4 (Turbo C: 2 → −32768…32767), long 4/8, float 4, double 8
- signed char −128…127; unsigned char 0…255; `sizeof('A')` = sizeof(int) in C
- Format specifiers: %d %i int, %u unsigned, %ld long, %f float/double (printf), %lf double (scanf), %c char, %s string, %o octal, %x hex, %e, %p pointer
- Constants: `const int N = 10;` or `#define N 10`; `void` = no value

questions.question: With 32-bit int, what does  unsigned int x = -1;  printf("%u", x);  print?
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: −1 converted to unsigned wraps to 2³² − 1.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In C, overflow of an unsigned integer wraps around modulo 2ⁿ.
II. In C, overflow of a signed int is guaranteed to wrap around the same way.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is modular by definition; signed overflow is undefined behaviour.

questions.question: After  int x = 3.9;  the value of x is:
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: Conversion from floating to integer truncates toward zero.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In C, the value of 5 % 3 is 2.
Reason (R): The % operator in C also accepts floating-point operands.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: % needs integer operands; fmod() is used for floating-point values.

questions.question: What is the value of  5 + 3 * 2  in C?
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: * has higher precedence than +: 5 + 6.

questions.question: What is the value of  10 / 3 * 3  in C (int operands)?
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: Left to right: 10 / 3 = 3 (integer division), 3 * 3 = 9.

questions.question: What is the value of  10 % 3 * 2 ?
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: % and * have equal precedence, left to right: 1 * 2 = 2.

questions.question: In C99, the values of  -7 / 2  and  -7 % 2  are:
questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion
questions.explanation: Division truncates toward zero, and (a/b)*b + a%b == a: (−3)(2) + (−1) = −7.

questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion

questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion

questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion

questions.question: What is the value of 5.0 / 2 in C?

options.C: float, because the int is converted

questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion

questions.subject: Type Declaration, Arithmetic Instructions and Type Conversion

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In C, sizeof is an operator, not a library function.
Reason (R): sizeof(int) can be evaluated by the compiler at compile time.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: Both true; sizeof is an operator by definition of the language, and compile-time evaluation is a consequence, not the reason.

questions.question: After  int i = 5, j;  j = i++ + 2;  the values of i and j are:
questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: i++ yields the old value 5 and then increments i.

questions.question: After  int a = 0, b = 5;  if (a && (b = 10)) ;  the value of b is:
questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: a is 0, so && short-circuits and the assignment b = 10 is never evaluated.

questions.question: After  int a = 1, b = 5;  if (a || b++) ;  the value of b is:
questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: a is non-zero, so || short-circuits and b++ is not evaluated.

questions.question: What is the value of x after  x = (1, 2, 3);
questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: The comma operator evaluates left to right and yields its last operand.

questions.question: What is the value of the expression  5 > 3 > 1  in C?
questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: (5 > 3) is 1, then 1 > 1 is 0.

questions.question: What is the value of  3 == 3 == 3  in C?

questions.question: How does C parse the expression  a & b == c ?

questions.question: In  a = b = c = 5;  the assignments are performed:

options.A: Right to left, so all three become 5
options.B: Left to right, so only a becomes 5

questions.subject: Operators, Hierarchy of Operators and Input-Output Statements
questions.explanation: Assignment is right-associative: a = (b = (c = 5)).

notes.title: C instructions and operators – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Instructions (Kanetkar)
- Type declaration, arithmetic, control instructions
- Arithmetic: variable on the left (`a + b = c` is invalid); `%` only for integers; no power operator – `pow()`
- int / int → int (5 / 2 = 2); one real operand → real (5.0 / 2 = 2.5); `float a = 5 / 2` → 2.0
- Assignment converts: `int k = 7.9 / 2` → 3; `char ch = 321` → 65
- Casts: `(float) a / b` = 3.5 but `(float)(a / b)` = 3.0 (a = 7, b = 2)
- C99: −7 / 2 = −3, −7 % 2 = −1 (sign of the dividend)

## Hierarchy of operators (high → low)
| Level | Operators | Assoc. |
|---|---|---|
| Postfix | `() [] -> .` `x++` | L→R |
| Unary | `! ~ ++ -- + - * & sizeof (type)` | R→L |
| Multiplicative | `* / %` | L→R |
| Additive | `+ -` | L→R |
| Shift | `<< >>` | L→R |
| Relational | `< <= > >=` | L→R |
| Equality | `== !=` | L→R |
| Bitwise | `&` then `^` then `|` | L→R |
| Logical | `&&` then `||` | L→R |
| Conditional | `?:` | R→L |
| Assignment | `= += -= …` | R→L |
| Comma | `,` | L→R |
- `&&` / `||` short-circuit; `5 > 3 > 1` = 0; `a & b == c` = `a & (b == c)`; `x = (1, 2, 3)` = 3
- Worked: `2*3/4 + 4/4 + 8 - 2 + 5/8` = 8; `10 + 20*3/4%5` = 10

## Input-output
- Formatted: `printf`, `scanf` (needs `&var`; returns the count read; `%s` stops at white space)
- Unformatted: `getchar putchar gets puts` (`getch getche` in conio.h)
- printf returns the number of characters printed (`printf("happy")` → 5); `%5.2f`, `%-5d`, `%%`

notes.title: Control structures – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Decisions
- `if`, `if-else`, nested if, `else if` ladder; non-zero = true, 0 = false; relational results are 1/0 (int)
- Traps: `if (x = 5)` is always true; `if (a > b);` has an empty body; without braces only one statement belongs to the if
- **Dangling else** pairs with the nearest unmatched `if`
- `10 <= x <= 20` is always true – write `x >= 10 && x <= 20`
- `&&`, `||` short-circuit (right side may not run: `i++ || j++`)
- `?:` – three operands, right-associative; `max = a > b ? a : b`
- Never compare floats with `==` (`0.1f != 0.1`)
- Leap year: `(y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0) || y % 400 == 0`

## Loops
| Loop | Test | Runs at least |
|---|---|---|
| while | before body | 0 times |
| for (init; test; update) | before body | 0 times (init once) |
| do … while( ); | after body | 1 time |
- `for (;;)` and `while (1)` are infinite; `for (i = 0; i < 5; i++);` – the `;` is the body (i ends at 5)
- `break` – leaves the innermost loop/switch; `continue` – next iteration; `goto label;` – jump within a function; `exit()` – ends the program
- Counting: `for (i = 1; i <= 100; i *= 2)` runs 7 times; `while (i++ < 5)` tests 6 times and leaves i = 6

## switch
- Expression and case labels must be integer types (int, char, enum) – no float, no ranges, no duplicates
- Without `break` control falls through to the next case; `default` may be anywhere

notes.title: Arrays and strings – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Arrays
- `int a[5];` indices 0–4; no bounds checking (a[5] or a[-1] → garbage / undefined)
- `int a[5] = {1, 2};` → rest 0; `int a[] = {…}` size from initialisers; count = `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])`
- 2-D row-major: address of a[i][j] = base + (i × cols + j) × size; `char a[100][100]` → a[40][50] at 4050
- `int a[3][2] = {1,2,3,4,5,6}` → a[2][1] = 6; `int a[2][3][4]` = 24 elements
- Array name = `&a[0]` (cannot be assigned: `a = b` is an error); `2[a]` = `a[2]`
- Bubble sort: n − 1 passes, n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, O(n²) (O(n) best with a swap flag); largest element moves to the end after each pass
  - [4,3,2,1,8,7,6,5] → pass 1: 3 2 1 4 7 6 5 8 → pass 2: 2 1 3 4 6 5 7 8

## Strings
- char array ending in `'\0'`; `"hi"` takes 3 bytes; `sizeof("bengaluru")` = 10, `strlen` = 9
- `char s[10]; s = "hi";` is an error – use `strcpy(s, "hi")`
- `<string.h>`: strlen, strcpy(dest, src), strncpy, strcat(dest, src), strncmp, strcmp (0 when equal), strchr (char), strstr (substring), strrev (Turbo C)
- `<ctype.h>`: toupper, tolower, isdigit, isalpha; `<stdlib.h>`: atoi, atof
- `scanf("%s")` stops at a space; `gets` removed (use `fgets`); compare contents with strcmp, not ==
- `'a' − 32 = 'A'`; palindrome: s[i] vs s[n − 1 − i]
